claims.text: Superconductivity in the proposed high-entropy-alloy class is primarily governed by average valence electron concentration (VEC).
Local chemical and structural disorder modulates the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states tune the electron–phonon interactions responsible for superconductivity.
The starting material is a single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
The starting material has a random elemental distribution with moderate local compositional fluctuations.
Substituting one constituent with an element of different valence will modify the alloy's overall VEC.
The proposed substitutions can be performed while retaining a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Controlling synthesis and using identical magnetic-field and pressure conditions will make Tc measurements across samples comparable.
Adjusting VEC changes the density of states at the Fermi level.
A higher density of states enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling favors a higher superconducting transition temperature.
A lower density of states suppresses superconductivity.
Lattice disorder modifies local electronic states and thereby affects superconducting pairing interactions.
Increasing VEC by substitution will raise Tc relative to the baseline if the single-phase solid solution is retained.
Reducing VEC by substitution will lower Tc relative to the baseline if the single-phase solid solution is retained.
The hypothesis applies only to single-phase, disordered solid solutions.
Phase separation, significant ordering, or substantial microstructural changes may mask or alter the influence of VEC on superconductivity.
Phonon spectra, residual strain, and microstructural inhomogeneity may also significantly affect superconductivity.
Failure of increased VEC to consistently raise Tc, or of reduced VEC to consistently lower Tc, would falsify the hypothesis.
A Tc variation associated with phase separation or ordering rather than VEC would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Phase separation or ordering is defined as outside the hypothesis's applicable boundary, but its occurrence is also presented as a falsifying outcome. An out-of-domain sample is ordinarily inconclusive rather than a direct falsification of a hypothesis restricted to retained single-phase disorder.
